715.title: The trustworthy
715.hook: Mecca calls him al-Amin and al-Sadiq, the trustworthy and the truthful
715.howItsDone: Muslims refer to the Prophet ﷺ as al-Sadiq al-Amin, the truthful and trustworthy, and honesty in speech and trade is taught as part of following his example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fudul, the pact to stand with the wronged. Your line was: defend the wronged.

Some reputations are built by speeches. This one, as the sirah tells it, was built the slow way, in the ordinary dealings of a trading town: what a person says, what a person keeps, what a person gives back. By the time the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is a grown man in Mecca, the sirah says, people have stopped using only his name. They call him by what he is to them: a title given not by a king, but by neighbors and traders. Today: the trustworthy.
screen: `NOT BUILT BY SPEECHES.` → `SMALL THINGS, DONE THE SAME WAY.` → `A TITLE FROM THE NEIGHBORS.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq says Quraysh called him al-Amin, the trustworthy. Tradition remembers him too as al-Sadiq, the truthful. Two words, one picture: a man whose word matched what happened, and whose hands could be trusted with what wasn't his. Muslims often point to two hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari where the praise comes from people who had turned against his message. The first comes from the day he began to call his own clans in public. He climbs the hill of Safa and calls them by name. When they gather, he asks: if I told you there were horsemen in the valley behind this hill, about to attack you, would you believe me? And they answer: yes, we have never known you to say anything but the truth. Then he tells them his message, and his own uncle Abu Lahab scolds him in front of everyone. But they had already said it. The second comes from Abu Sufyan, at the time still one of his fiercest opponents, standing before the Byzantine emperor Heraclius, who questions him about this new prophet. Did you ever accuse him of lying, before he made his claim? And Abu Sufyan says no. In the same report he admits he'd have lied about him if he hadn't feared his companions calling him a liar. Heraclius reasons aloud: a man who never lied about people would hardly lie about God. Both scenes come from after the revelation began, but both look back. Even his opponents say that before the message, they had known him for his word. The trust was there first.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a moment coming up where the easy thing is a small untruth, an excuse for being late, a compliment you don't mean, a number rounded the convenient way, and picture yourself saying the true thing instead, kindly and plainly. Rehearse the sentence once in your head until it feels like yours. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make your word match your deed.

716.title: Khadijah's caravan
716.hook: she sends him to Syria with her goods and her servant Maysarah, who returns full of praise
716.howItsDone: Muslims remember Khadijah as a respected merchant and as the Prophet's ﷺ first wife, and honesty in trade is taught from his example and from hadith such as the one on the truthful, trustworthy merchant.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the trustworthy: al-Amin, known for his word. Your line was: known for truth. That closes the childhood and youth. Now, a new part: Khadijah and the household.
screen: `KNOWN FOR TRUTH.` → `NOW: KHADIJAH AND THE HOUSEHOLD.`

segments.voice: A merchant in Mecca has goods to send north, and she doesn't travel with them. Whoever carries them will be out of her sight for a long time, buying and selling with her money in markets far from Mecca. She needs someone she can trust completely, someone who will bring back every coin, and she has heard a name. The merchant is a woman, Khadijah bint Khuwaylid. Today: Khadijah's caravan.
screen: `GOODS TO SEND NORTH.` → `OUT OF HER SIGHT FOR A LONG TIME.` → `A WOMAN OF TRADE.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq describes Khadijah as a merchant woman of honor and wealth, who hired men to trade with her goods for a share of the profit. She has heard about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: his truthfulness, his trustworthiness, his character. Yesterday's title has traveled. So she sends him an offer. Take my goods to Syria, she says, and I'll give you more than I give the others. And she sends her servant Maysarah with him. He accepts. The caravan goes north. He trades, sells what he brought, buys what she wanted, and comes back to Mecca. The sirah says the business did well. But the profit isn't what the story lingers on. It lingers on Maysarah, who has spent the whole journey beside him, seeing him far from home: in the heat, at the market, at the haggling table where small dishonesties are easy. When they return, Maysarah goes to Khadijah and tells her what he saw. Ibn Ishaq says his report included wonders: a monk's words about him, and angels Maysarah saw shading him from the sun. That's the turn. The goods came back. So did a report, and it was about the man, not the profit. The Qur'an's word for something handed over like this is amanah, a trust. In surah four, Pickthall translates: "Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners." He restored hers, and more. Later, in a hadith collected by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet says the truthful, trustworthy merchant will be with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs. A merchant, in that company.

Notice the one corner you'd usually cut, the shortcut nobody would notice, and choose, now, to do that part well. If you pray, you can ask Allah for honest hands; if not, just hold the choice.

717.title: She proposed
717.hook: Khadijah, respected and independent, proposes marriage through a friend
717.howItsDone: Muslims remember Khadijah as Umm al-Mu'minin, a mother of the believers, and her proposal is often retold in talks on marriage and on the dignity of women in the Prophet's ﷺ life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khadijah's caravan. Her goods went north to Syria, and Maysarah came home talking about the man who led it. Your line was: his honesty was the report.

A message leaves a merchant's house in Mecca, carried quietly by a friend. It comes from a woman of standing, with her own wealth and her own trade. It goes to a young man with no fortune at all. She has heard Maysarah's report about the man who led her caravan, weighed it, and made up her mind. The friend's question sounds casual: what's keeping him from marriage? It isn't casual at all. Today: she proposed.
screen: `A MESSAGE FROM A MERCHANT'S HOUSE.` → `TO A MAN WITH NO FORTUNE.` → `SHE PROPOSED.`

segments.voice: Khadijah wasn't marrying for money; she had her own goods on the road and men hired to trade them. What she was choosing was a person. In Ibn Ishaq's telling, she sends word to him with her reasons: the family tie between them, his good name among his people, his trustworthiness, his character, his truthfulness. Not his money; he had little. Another report, in Ibn Sa'd, says she first sent a friend, a woman named Nafisa, to ask him quietly what was keeping him from marriage. He said he had nothing to marry with. And Nafisa asked: and if that were taken care of, and you were invited by beauty, wealth, standing and a good match? So the go-between opened the door, and Khadijah walked through it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his uncles, the families met, and the marriage was made. The sources give different names for who spoke for her family; they agree on who asked first. Much later, the Qur'an describes what a marriage is meant to hold. In Pickthall's words: "He ordained between you love and mercy." And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari answers her choice from the other side. Years on, the angel Jibril comes to the Prophet and says: Khadijah is on her way to you with a dish of food. When she arrives, give her greetings of peace from her Lord, and from me. A woman who chose, and was greeted by name.

718.title: Their children
718.hook: Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah, and sons who died in infancy
718.howItsDone: Muslims who lose a child say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un and pray for the family; the Prophet's ﷺ name Abu al-Qasim, after a son who died young, is still used of him today.

segments.voice: Yesterday: she proposed. Khadijah asked him herself, for the sake of his character. Your line was: she chose him.

Abu al-Qasim. Father of Qasim. It's a kunya, a name built from a child's name, a way of calling a man through his child. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was called by this one, and it is still used of him today. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari even has him say: call yourselves by my name, but not by my kunya. And Qasim himself? A little boy who did not live to grow up. His father carried his name anyway.
screen: `FATHER OF SO-AND-SO.` → `ABU AL-QASIM.` → `A LITTLE BOY WHO DIED.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq lists the children Khadijah bore him. Sons first: al-Qasim, then the names al-Tayyib and al-Tahir, the good one and the pure one. Some scholars read those two names as one son, called Abdullah, with two titles; the sources don't settle it. Ibn Ishaq says simply that the sons died before Islam came. Then the daughters, each with her own story still ahead: Zaynab. Ruqayyah. Umm Kulthum. Fatimah. Ibn Ishaq says they lived to see Islam, accepted it, and emigrated with their father. Here traditions read the record in more than one way. Sunni tradition counts all four as daughters of the Prophet and Khadijah. Some Shia scholars hold that Fatimah alone was their daughter by birth, and that the others were raised in the house; other Shia scholars accept all four. And of Fatimah, her father says in Sahih al-Bukhari: Fatimah is a part of me. Put it together and the house in Mecca comes into view: a mother who traded, a father who was trusted, girls growing up, and small graves too. Grief came into that home before any revelation. And the sources keep every name, even the boys who died small. One more picture, from a long dream the Prophet describes in Sahih al-Bukhari. He sees the prophet Ibrahim in a garden, and around him, children. He's told they are the children who died young. Every child remembered.

719.title: Zayd chooses
719.hook: Zayd, a freed boy in the house, chooses to stay with him rather than go home with his own father
719.howItsDone: Muslims remember Zayd ibn Harithah as a beloved companion of the Prophet ﷺ, and his story is told when teaching about the Qur'an's ruling that adopted children keep their birth parents' names.

segments.voice: Yesterday: their children. Four daughters, and little sons who died, whose names the sources keep. Your line was: every child remembered.

A father has been looking for his son for a long time. The boy was taken in a raid, the sirah says, and sold in a market far from home. The father mourned him in verse: I weep for Zayd, and I don't know what became of him. Then word comes. The boy is alive, in Mecca, in the house of a man of Quraysh, Muhammad ibn Abdullah. The father and his brother ride south with money to buy him back. They find him. And the boy says no.
screen: `A BOY TAKEN IN A RAID.` → `A FATHER WEEPS IN VERSE.` → `THE BOY SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: Here's how the sirah tells it. Zayd ibn Harithah came into the house as a gift. Khadijah's nephew had bought him, she received him, and she gave him to her husband, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. When Zayd's father, Harithah, arrived with the ransom, the Prophet didn't haggle. He said, in the account Ibn Sa'd keeps: call him, and let him choose. If he chooses you, he's yours, with no price. If he chooses me, I'm not a man to turn away someone who chooses me. So they called Zayd. Do you know these men? Yes, my father and my uncle. And Zayd said: I won't choose anyone over you. His father was stunned. You'd choose slavery over your own father and family? Zayd answered that he had seen something in this man he would never trade. Then the Prophet took him by the hand to the gathering place by the Ka'ba and said: bear witness, Zayd is my son. The father, the report says, went home at peace. People called him Zayd ibn Muhammad until a verse came, Sahih al-Bukhari records, and Pickthall renders its opening: "Proclaim their real parentage." So he was Zayd ibn Harithah again, his own father's son. But the bond stayed, and the Qur'an, at surah thirty-three, verse thirty-seven, mentions Zayd by name. A boy who chose a house, kept in the Book.

720.title: Ali in the house
720.hook: young Ali, Abu Talib's son, is raised in the Prophet's home
720.howItsDone: Muslims who sponsor or care for orphans often recall the Prophet's ﷺ words about the two fingers side by side, and Ali's upbringing in his home is told when Muslims remember Ali.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zayd chose. Offered his father's home, he stayed, and was called a son. Your line was: he chose to stay.

A hard year comes to Mecca. Ibn Ishaq calls it a severe famine, and says it hit Quraysh badly. One house feels it hard: Abu Talib's. He's the uncle who took in an orphaned nephew years before and gave him a place at the table. Now Abu Talib has a big family and not enough to feed them. And the nephew, grown now and married to Khadijah, has an idea. Today: Ali in the house.

segments.voice: Day seven hundred eleven gave this plan in a sentence. Here it is up close, as Ibn Ishaq tells it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ goes to another uncle, al-Abbas: your brother Abu Talib has a large family, and you can see how hard things are. Let's lighten his load. I'll take one of his sons, you take one. Al-Abbas agrees, and they ask Abu Talib together. So two boys change houses that year. Al-Abbas takes Ja'far. The Prophet takes Ali, a small boy, into his home with Khadijah, where he joins Zayd, the boy who chose to stay. A household that keeps making room. Ibn Ishaq says Ali stayed with him from then on, and when revelation came, Ali followed him and believed. Later, the paths read Ali's place in more than one way. Sunni tradition counts him among the rightly guided caliphs; Shia tradition holds him to be the Imam after the Prophet. But here he is still a child at Khadijah's table. Ali wasn't an orphan; his father was alive. The man who took him in had been one, though. And in Sahih al-Bukhari, that man says the one who looks after an orphan will be with him in Paradise like this, holding up two fingers side by side. The house that raised Ali was run by someone who knew what that care was worth.

segments.voice: Think of a child in your world who isn't yours, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, or of an adult who did that for you when you were small. Ask one plain question: what would lighten the load? A meal, a ride, an hour, a kind word to a tired parent; if you pray, pray for that child by name.

721.title: The black stone lifted together
721.hook: at thirty-five he settles the tribes' quarrel over the stone with a cloak (sirah)
721.howItsDone: Pilgrims circling the Ka'ba pass outside the curved wall of the Hijr, and touch, kiss or gesture toward the Black Stone, following the Prophet's ﷺ example.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ali. In a hard year, Abu Talib's son came to live with the Prophet and Khadijah. Your line was: raised in that house.

Before the quarrel, there was a rule about money. The Ka'ba was old and damaged, and the clans of Quraysh agreed to pull it down and build it again. Ibn Ishaq says one of their elders stood up and told them: put nothing into this House but clean money. Nothing earned from usury, nothing from prostitution, nothing taken unjustly from anyone. They agreed, and built, clan by clan, wall by wall. Today: al-Amin.
screen: `AN OLD HOUSE, DAMAGED.` → `ONLY CLEAN MONEY.` → `CLAN BY CLAN, WALL BY WALL.`

segments.voice: Clean money ran short. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, from 'Aishah, says the Prophet told her that her people's funds fell short, and so a part of the old House was left outside the new walls. That's the space behind the low curved wall on one side of the Ka'ba, the Hijr. Pilgrims circle outside it, because it belongs to the House. The Qur'an remembers who raised the House's foundations. Pickthall's words: "And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House." So the clans were rebuilding, imperfectly, something they believed Ibrahim had begun. Then came the corner where the Black Stone sits, and every clan wanted the honor of setting it in place. Ibn Ishaq says the quarrel went on for days, and the clans came close to fighting. They agreed to let the next man through the gate decide. It was the one they called al-Amin, the trustworthy; Ibn Ishaq says he was thirty-five. He asked for a cloak, laid the stone on it, and had a man from each clan take hold of the edge. They lifted it together, and he set it in the wall with his own hand. That closes a week in the household: the trustworthy one, Khadijah's caravan, her proposal, their children, Zayd, Ali, and a cloak with room for every hand. Next comes the mountain, and the revelation.

segments.voice: Think of a disagreement near you, at work, at home, in a group chat, where each side wants the honor or the last word. Don't pick a winner; picture the cloak instead, and let one small, practical idea come that would let every person take hold of an edge. If you pray, ask for wisdom in it.
